title: Born knowing and learning: what animals can do from birth, and what they learn

summary.text: A baby spider spins her first web with no one to show her how. Some things an animal can do from the day they are born, with no teaching. This is called instinct. Other things an animal learns, by trying again and again, or by watching others. Humans are animals too: a newborn baby grips your finger without being taught, but has to learn to talk. Your child tests their own knee kick, a born-with action, to find out whether they can stop it by trying.
summary.art: A small brown spider spinning a round web on a balcony grill at dusk, and inside the flat a girl holding out her finger to a newborn baby who grips her finger tight.

intro.hook: Many spider mothers leave before their babies hatch. Nobody ever shows the babies how to spin a web. Yet each one spins a web of the right shape. How does she know how?
intro.text: Some things you could do on the day you were born. You could cry, drink milk and hold a finger tight. Nobody taught you. Other things you learned later, like talking and brushing your teeth. Other animals are the same. A spider is born ready to spin. A kitten learns to hunt by watching her mother. In this unit you meet animals who are born knowing, and animals who learn. Then you test a born-with action in your own body: can you stop it if you try?
intro.art: Two halves of one picture: on the left a newborn baby gripping a grown-up's finger, on the right the same child, now seven, wobbling on a cycle with a grown-up holding the seat.

outcomes: By the end I can say that some things an animal can do from birth, with no teaching, and that this is called instinct.
By the end I can say that other things an animal learns, by trying again and again or by watching others.
By the end I can give examples of both in humans and other animals: a spider spins a web by instinct, and a child learns to talk.
By the end I can say that many things are both: an animal is born ready to do them and gets better with practice.
By the end I can make a guess with a reason, test whether I can stop my knee kick by trying, count my results and say what I found.
By the end I can say that a reflex is a quick action the body does by itself, like a knee kick or a sneeze.

terms.meaning: An instinct is something an animal can do from birth, without being taught.
terms.example: A baby spider spins her first web by instinct. Nobody shows her how.
terms.art: A tiny spiderling on a twig, spinning a small round web, with no other spider anywhere near.

terms.meaning: Learning is getting a new skill or knowing something new, by trying, by watching others or by being taught.
terms.example: A child learns to speak Kannada by hearing her family speak Kannada every day.
terms.art: An older woman and a small girl talking on a doorstep in Mysuru, with speech bubbles between them.

terms.meaning: Practice means doing something again and again, so that you get better at it.
terms.example: Your first kolam may be wobbly. After a week of drawing one every morning, the lines get straighter.
terms.art: Three kolams drawn in a row on a doorstep: the first wobbly, the second better, the third neat and even.

terms.meaning: A reflex is a very quick action that the body does by itself, before you decide to do it.
terms.example: When something flies at your face, you blink. When dust tickles your nose, you sneeze. Both are reflexes.
terms.art: A boy blinking hard as a paper ball flies towards his face, and a girl sneezing at a dusty shelf.

terms.meaning: A spiderling is a baby spider, just come out of the egg.
terms.example: Spiderlings come out of a silk egg bag. Each spiderling goes off alone, and spins her own web.
terms.art: A round silk egg bag split open on a leaf, with many tiny spiderlings climbing out.

terms.meaning: A hatchling is a baby animal who has just come out of an egg.
terms.example: Olive ridley turtle hatchlings dig out of the sand on Odisha's beaches and crawl straight to the sea.
terms.art: Small dark turtle hatchlings crawling over sand towards the white edge of the sea at night.

terms.meaning: Genes are tiny instructions inside every living body. Parents pass them on to their young.
terms.example: A spider's genes, passed on from her parents, help her body build a web of the right shape.
terms.art: A mother spider beside her silk egg bag, with soft glowing lines running from her to the tiny eggs inside.

explanations.context: This card is about the things an animal can do from the day they are born.
explanations.definition: An instinct is something an animal can do from birth, the first time, without being taught.
explanations.description: In many kinds of spider, the mother lays her eggs in a silk bag and leaves. The spiderlings hatch alone. Yet each one spins a web of the right shape for her kind. A newborn calf stands up and walks within a few hours. A turtle hatchling crawls towards the sea the moment she comes out of the sand. Human babies have instincts too. A newborn baby turns her head to a touch on the cheek, and sucks to drink milk. The know-how for an instinct comes from the parents, passed on in the body. Scientists say it is carried in genes, the tiny instructions inside every cell.
examples: A spiderling spins her first web with no teacher.
A newborn calf stands up and walks on the day he is born.
A newborn baby sucks to drink milk, and grips a finger tight.
Olive ridley turtle hatchlings crawl to the sea at night.
explanations.art: Four small pictures: a spiderling spinning, a wobbly calf standing beside his mother, a baby drinking milk, and turtle hatchlings on sand.

explanations.concept: Learned: by trying and by watching
explanations.context: This card is about the things an animal has to learn after they are born.
explanations.definition: Learning is getting a new skill or new knowledge after birth, by trying again and again, by watching others or by being taught.
explanations.description: Some things nobody is born knowing. A kitten is born with the urge to pounce. But she learns which animals to hunt, and how, from watching her mother and from many tries. A crow learns which balcony puts out rice every morning, and flies there at the right time. A child is not born knowing Tamil, Bengali or English. She learns the words her family speaks around her. Learning takes time and practice. The first tries are often wrong, and each try teaches something.
examples: A kitten learns to hunt by watching her mother and trying.
A crow learns which window puts out rice, and comes back every day.
A child learns the language her family speaks.
A child learns to ride a cycle after many falls.
explanations.art: A mother cat crouching to pounce on a leaf, with her kitten crouched beside her copying.

explanations.context: This card is about actions that an animal is born ready for, and then gets better at with practice.
explanations.definition: Many actions start as an instinct and get better with practice. Instinct and learning work together.
explanations.description: A chick pecks at grains on the day she hatches. Nobody teaches her, but she misses many grains at first. After a few days she hits more of them. Weaver birds are born ready to weave a nest of grass. Elsie Collias and her husband Nicholas, scientists in the United States, studied the village weaver, an African cousin of the baya. Young males weave untidy nests at first, and get better with practice. A human baby is born moving her legs in steps when she is held up. But walking takes about a year of falling and trying again. Every baby is born ready to learn a language, but the one she speaks depends on what she hears.
examples: A chick pecks from birth, and her aim gets better with practice.
A weaver bird is born ready to weave, and young males' nests get neater with practice.
A baby is born ready to learn a language, but learns the one she hears.
explanations.art: A row of three hanging grass nests on a palm leaf: one messy, one better, one neat, with a yellow-headed baya weaver bird at the neat one.

explanations.context: This card explains your knee kick. Read it after the stop test.
explanations.definition: A reflex is a very quick action the body does by itself. It happens before you decide to do it.
explanations.description: When someone taps just below your kneecap, the tap stretches the big muscle on the front of your leg. A message runs from that muscle up to your backbone. Inside your backbone is your spinal cord, a thick bundle of nerves. The message comes straight back down to the muscle, and the muscle tightens. Your leg kicks. All this happens in a tiny part of a second, before you decide anything. That is why trying hard to stop it often does not work. You can hold your leg stiff against it, but you cannot simply switch it off. You were born with this kick. Babies, children and grandmothers all have it. Blinking at dust and sneezing are reflexes too.
examples: The knee kick when the spot below the kneecap is tapped.
A sneeze when dust tickles your nose.
Pulling your hand back from a hot tawa before you even feel it hurt.
explanations.art: A child sitting on a bed edge with legs hanging, a grown-up tapping just below the kneecap, and an arrow showing a message going from the knee to the backbone and back.

explanations.context: This card is about a real argument: when an animal acts by instinct, is the animal thinking?
explanations.description: A spider is born knowing how to spin. But she still makes many choices. She picks a place for her web, such as a corner where flies come. She fixes holes after the wind. In 1973, two garden spiders were taken to a space station, where nothing has weight. Arabella's first web was messy. Her next webs were much more like the webs spiders spin on Earth. So she seemed to change what she did, to suit a strange new place. Scientists agree on what spiders do. They argue about what goes on inside the spider while she spins.
examples: A spider chooses the corner for her web.
A spider mends a hole in her web.
Arabella, a spider in space, spun better webs after her first messy one.

perspectives.explanation: An instinct gives the spider her know-how, and her mind uses that know-how. She senses the place, decides where to fix each thread and changes her plan when something goes wrong. Born know-how and thinking work together.
An instinct is a set of steps built into the body, and it runs the same way every time it is switched on. They prefer to say that the spider responds, not that she thinks.

explanations.art: A garden spider in the middle of a round web inside a small metal box floating in a space station, with an astronaut watching through the glass.

agreed.text: Some actions animals can do from birth, with no teaching. Spiders spin webs, newborn calves stand, and human babies suck and grip.
agreed.evidence: Spiderlings that hatch alone, away from any other spider, still spin the web shape of their own kind. Doctors check a newborn baby's grip and sucking on the first day.

agreed.text: Many things are learned after birth, such as which foods are safe, where food can be found and which language to speak.
agreed.evidence: Children speak the language they hear around them as babies, whatever language their parents' parents spoke. Crows and pigeons come to the places where people feed them every day.

agreed.text: Many born-with actions get better with practice.
agreed.evidence: Scientists who counted a chick's pecks found that newly hatched chicks miss many grains, and miss fewer after a few days of pecking. Elsie and Nicholas Collias, scientists in the United States, found in the 1960s that young male village weavers weave better with practice.

challenging.claim: A newborn baby knows nothing at all. Everything has to be learned.
challenging.who: John Locke, an English thinker, in 1690, and many people since
challenging.for: Babies cannot talk, walk or feed themselves, and almost everything a grown-up does was learned.
challenging.against: Newborn babies already suck, grip, cry and turn to a touch on the cheek. Babies a few months old can hear the difference between sounds from many languages, which grown-ups often cannot. A baby is born ready to do some things and ready to learn others.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea: that a baby's mind starts empty.

challenging.claim: Something done by instinct is done perfectly the first time.
challenging.for: A spiderling spins a web of the right shape with no teacher, and a calf stands on his first day.
challenging.against: A chick's first pecks miss many grains, and her aim gets better over a few days. Young weaver birds build messy nests at first. Arabella the spider spun a messy web in space before she spun better ones.
challenging.context: This card is about whether born-with actions can still get better.

challenging.claim: Other animals act by instinct, and only humans learn.
challenging.for: Humans learn a huge amount: languages, reading, cooking, music.
challenging.against: Humans have instincts too, like sucking and gripping as babies, and reflexes like the knee kick. And other animals learn all the time. A crow learns which window gives rice, and a kitten learns to hunt from her mother.
challenging.context: This card is about whether humans and other animals are different in how they come to know things.

challenging.claim: When an animal acts by instinct, the animal is not thinking.
challenging.who: Some scientists, for over a hundred years
challenging.for: An instinct can run in the same steps every time, even in an animal who has never seen the job done.
challenging.against: Animals use their instincts with choices: a spider picks her web's place and mends holes, and Arabella changed her webs in space. Many scientists say instinct and thinking work together.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument among scientists.

big_questions.q: Nobody taught the spider to spin. So where did her know-how come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about her mother, and her mother's mother. What did each spider pass on to her babies, even without meeting them?

big_questions.q: In the stop test, why was the kick so hard to stop, even though it is your own leg?
big_questions.hint: Where does the message from your knee go? Does it wait for you to decide?

big_questions.q: A chick is born pecking, but her aim gets better. Is pecking born or learned?
big_questions.hint: Could it be a bit of both? Which part came with her, and which part did she work out?

big_questions.q: If you had grown up in a different family far away, which things about you would be the same, and which would be different?
big_questions.hint: Think of your language, your favourite food, your knee kick and the way you sneeze.

big_questions.q: Are the things you were born knowing really yours, or did you get them from everyone before you?
big_questions.hint: Your parents passed on genes from their parents, and they from theirs. Is a gift from long ago still yours?

story.title: The Grip and the Web
story.note: A made-up story. The facts in it are true: newborn babies grip a finger tight, the knee kick happens by itself at every age, and many spiders that spin round webs build them at dusk and rebuild them in the same place.
text: Kayal lived on the third floor of a building in Visakhapatnam. She was seven. Her little brother Sabari was five. Their grandmother, Ammamma, lived with them.

One Sunday, Pinni came to visit. Pinni was their mother's younger sister. That is what a mother's younger sister is called in Telugu. She carried a bundle wrapped in a soft cotton towel. Inside was baby Nila, only two weeks old.
Kayal sat very still on the sofa, and Pinni laid Nila in her lap. Nila's fingers were tiny and pink. Kayal put one finger into Nila's open hand.
At once, the little fingers closed around hers. Nila held on tight. Kayal gently lifted her finger, and Nila still did not let go.
'She is so strong!' said Kayal. 'Who taught her to hold on like that?'
'Nobody,' said Pinni. 'Every baby is born able to grip. Nila also knew how to drink milk on her very first day. Doctors check for that grip when a baby is born.'
Kayal thought about this. Then she waved her hand slowly in front of Nila's face. 'Bye-bye, Nila. Wave bye-bye!'
Nila just looked at her with big dark eyes. Her hands stayed still.
'She cannot wave yet,' said Pinni, laughing. 'Waving is not something babies are born with. She will learn it in a year or so, by watching all of you.'
Sabari was jumping on the other end of the sofa. 'I can whistle!' he said, and he whistled a wobbly tune. 'Nobody taught me. I was born whistling.'
Ammamma laughed so much that her glasses slipped. 'Born whistling? You puffed and puffed on the balcony for two whole weeks. Nothing came out but air and spit.'
'Oh,' said Sabari. 'Then I learned it.'
'You learned it by practice,' said Ammamma. 'Some things we are born knowing. Other things we learn.'
That evening, after Pinni and Nila went home, Kayal went out to the balcony. The sky was turning orange. Between two bars of the balcony grill and the jasmine pot, something was moving.
There was a small brown spider. She was dropping down on a thin silk thread, then climbing back up and across. Kayal fetched Ammamma's torch and called everyone.

They watched without touching. First the spider made lines from the middle outwards, like the spokes of a cycle wheel. Then she walked round and round the spokes, laying down a spiral of thread. Round and round she went, the circles getting closer together.
'She has done it so neatly,' whispered Kayal. 'Did her mother teach her?'
'In many kinds of spider, the mother lays her eggs in a silk bag and goes away,' said Ammamma. 'The babies come out alone. Each little one spins her first web by herself, with nobody to copy.'
'So the spider was born knowing how to spin,' said Kayal. 'Like Nila was born knowing how to grip.'
The next morning, the web was gone. Only a few broken threads were left on the grill. But that evening, at the same time, the spider was back in the same place, spinning a new web.
'She does this every day?' asked Sabari.
'Many spiders like her spin a new web every evening,' said Ammamma.
Kayal watched for a long time. 'Ammamma, can she get better at it? Or is a born-with thing always the same?'
Ammamma did not answer. Instead she said, 'Sabari, sit up on the dining table. Let your legs hang down.'
Sabari climbed up. Ammamma felt for the soft spot just below his kneecap. She gave it a gentle tap with the side of her hand.
Sabari's leg kicked forward by itself. Sabari's mouth fell open. 'I did not do that!' he shouted. 'My leg did it!'
Everyone laughed. Then Kayal tapped Ammamma's knee, very gently. Ammamma's leg kicked too.
'Even you, Ammamma!' said Kayal.
'Even me, at seventy-one,' said Ammamma. 'Nila has this kick too. We were all born with it.'
Kayal looked at her own knee. 'My leg kicks without me deciding,' she said slowly. 'Just like Nila grips without deciding.'
She frowned. 'But it is my leg. If I try really, really hard, can I stop it from kicking?'
'What do you think?' asked Ammamma.
'I don't know,' said Kayal. 'But I can find out.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kayal notices two kinds of know-how side by side: the baby's grip, the spider's web and the knee kick, which nobody taught, and waving and whistling, which have to be learned. The story ends on a real question that the stop test will answer: can you stop a born-with action just by trying?
ask: What could baby Nila do that nobody had taught her?
How did Ammamma know that Sabari was not born whistling?
Who taught the spider to spin her web?

A small boy on a balcony puffing out his cheeks, trying to whistle, while his grandmother laughs with her glasses slipping.

experiments.title: The Stop Test: can you stop your knee kick by trying?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up taps just below your kneecap, 5 times in each of three ways. First you just relax. Then you try as hard as you can not to kick. Then you hook your fingers together and pull hard. You count the kicks and how big they are each time.
experiments.question: Can you stop a born-with action, like your knee kick, just by trying hard?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When you try as hard as you can not to kick, will your leg still kick? And when you pull your hooked fingers hard, will the kick be smaller, the same or bigger? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same grown-up taps the same spot below the same knee, gently, with the side of the hand, 5 times in each way. You always look away, so that you cannot see the tap coming. We use 5 taps each time, because one tap can miss the spot.
results_table: How big: none, small or big

materials.item: a bed, a dining table or a strong table, high enough for your feet to hang free
a pencil and paper for the results table

experiments.safety: Tap gently, with the side of the hand, on the soft spot just below the kneecap. Never tap the kneecap itself, and never hit hard. Stand to the side of the foot, because the leg kicks forward.

schedule.what: Guess, then tap 5 times in each of three ways, count the kicks, test a grown-up's knee, and talk about what happened.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table for the three ways. Draw your leg three times, with a short arrow for a small kick and a long arrow for a big kick.

setup.art: A girl sitting on the edge of a bed with her legs hanging free, looking away, while a grown-up taps gently just below her kneecap with the side of her hand.
setup.caption: 1. Relax and look away. A grown-up taps just below your kneecap, 5 times.

setup.art: The same girl with her face screwed up, trying hard to keep her leg still, as a grown-up taps her knee.
setup.caption: 2. Now try as hard as you can not to kick. 5 more taps.

setup.art: The same girl with the fingers of both hands hooked together in front of her chest, pulling hard outwards, while her knee is tapped and her foot swings forward.
setup.caption: 3. Hook your fingers together and pull hard. 5 more taps.

setup.art: A results table on paper with three rows, 'Relaxed', 'Trying to stop' and 'Pulling fingers', and columns for kicks out of 5 and how big.
setup.caption: 4. Write down the kicks and how big they were.

flow.do: 1. Find a bed or table where your child can sit with feet hanging free. 2. Draw the results table on the paper. Your child can tell you what to write.
flow.say: Your knee has a born-with action. Nobody taught it to you. Today we find out if you are the boss of it.
flow.kid: Sit where your feet hang free. Let your legs hang loose.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess, and why. Write the guess on the paper.
flow.say: When I tap your knee and you try hard not to kick, will your leg still kick? And if you pull your fingers hard, what will the kick do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Can you stop the kick if you try? Why?

good: I can stop it, because it is my leg and I move it.
I cannot stop it, because the boy's leg in the story kicked by itself.
Pulling will make it smaller, because I will be busy.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine, as long as there is a reason. Do not tell your child what will happen.

flow.do: Way 1, relaxed: 1. Your child looks away and lets the leg hang loose. 2. Tap gently just below the kneecap, 5 times, a few seconds apart. 3. Count the kicks and say how big they were.
flow.say: Look away at the window. Let your leg hang like a wet towel. I will tap five times.
flow.kid: Look away. Let your leg hang loose. Count the kicks with your grown-up.
flow.parent: Feel for the soft spot just below the kneecap, in the middle. Use a quick, light tap, not a slow push. If nothing happens, move a finger-width up or down. A small kick moves the foot less than a finger's length. A big kick swings it further. Some people have only a small kick, which is normal. If one knee will not kick, try the other knee.

flow.do: Way 2, trying to stop: 1. Your child looks away and tries as hard as they can not to kick. 2. Tap 5 times. 3. Count the kicks and say how big they were.
flow.say: Now try as hard as you can to keep your leg still. Don't let it kick! I will tap five times.
flow.kid: Look away. Try your hardest not to kick. Count the kicks.
flow.parent: Many children still kick on some taps, though the kick may be smaller. Some can nearly stop it by making the leg stiff. If that happens, ask: did you switch the kick off, or did you hold your leg stiff against it?

flow.do: Way 3, pulling: 1. Your child hooks the fingers of both hands together in front of the chest. 2. Just before each tap, say 'Pull!' and they pull their hands apart hard. 3. Tap 5 times. 4. Count the kicks and say how big they were.
flow.say: Hook your fingers together like this. When I say 'pull', pull your hands apart hard, and keep looking away.
flow.kid: Hook your fingers. When you hear 'pull', pull hard. Count the kicks.

ask.q: What did your leg do this time?
good: It kicked bigger, and I was not even thinking about my leg.

flow.parent: Pulling the hooked fingers usually makes the kick bigger. Doctors use this trick when a kick is hard to see. It works because the busy arms stop you from holding your leg stiff.

flow.do: Let your child tap your knee 5 times, gently, while you relax and look away.
flow.say: Now you tap my knee. Gently, on the soft spot. Does my leg kick too?
flow.kid: Now tap your grown-up's knee. Gently! Does their leg kick?
flow.parent: Most grown-ups kick too, at any age. The kick is the same kind of action in a baby, a child and an old person.

flow.do: Ask what your child thinks, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Look at your table. Could you stop the kick by trying? When was it biggest? Why do you think that happened?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Could you stop the kick? When was it biggest?

ask.q: Why is the kick so hard to stop?
good: It happens before I decide anything.
The message goes from my knee to my backbone and back, without asking me.
I was born with it, so it works by itself.

check.q: In the stop test, what usually happens when you try hard not to kick?
options: The leg never kicks
The leg often still kicks, maybe smaller
The leg kicks much bigger
check.why: Most children still kick on some taps, though the kick may be smaller, because the kick happens before you decide. If you picked 'never kicks', did you stop the kick, or hold your leg stiff against it?

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the numbers: 'Relaxed, I kicked 5 times. Trying to stop, I still kicked 3 times, but small. Pulling, I kicked 5 big kicks.' Now read the card on reflexes.

activities.title: Web Watch: a web that nobody taught (if you find a web)
activities.context: In this activity you look for a spider web in your home or on the balcony, and look closely at the pattern. The spider spun this with no teacher.

materials.item: a magnifying glass, or a phone camera zoomed in

activities.safety: Look, but do not touch the spider or break the web.

schedule.what: Find a web, shine a torch on it, draw the pattern and look for the spider.

activities.record: A drawing of the web, with the spider drawn where you found her.

setup.art: A torch beam lighting up a round spider web between two bars of a balcony grill at dusk, with the threads shining.
setup.caption: 1. Look for a web in corners, behind cupboards or on the balcony grill. Shine a torch from the side.

setup.art: A notebook drawing of a round web with spokes and a spiral, and a messy tangle web from a ceiling corner beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the pattern you see.

flow.do: Search together: ceiling corners, behind cupboards, window frames, balcony grills and plant pots. Shine the torch from the side, so the threads shine.
flow.say: Spiders spin webs in quiet corners. Let's look. Shine the torch from the side. Can you see the threads?
flow.kid: Look in corners and on the balcony. Shine the torch from the side.
flow.parent: Most flats have at least one web in a corner. House spiders often spin messy tangle webs. Spiders that spin round webs are more often on balconies and in plants, and many spin at dusk. If you find no web, try again at dusk tomorrow, when round webs are spun.

flow.do: Your child draws the web. Look for spokes, a spiral, or a tangle.
flow.say: Is this web round, with spokes and a spiral, or a messy tangle? Draw what you see.
flow.kid: Draw the web. Is it round, or a tangle?

flow.do: Talk about who taught the spider.
flow.say: Most spider mothers are not there to teach their babies. Each kind of spider spins the web of her own kind. How do you think she knows how?
flow.kid: Who taught this spider? How does she know how to spin?
flow.think: If you saw a round web and a tangle web, were they spun by the same kind of spider?

activities.title: A Newborn's Grip (only if there is a baby under three months in the family)
activities.context: In this activity, if there is a very young baby in the family or among friends, you gently feel the grip that every baby is born with. Do this only with the parent's permission.
activities.safety: Wash your hands with soap first. Only do this with the baby's parent there, and when the baby is calm and awake. Never pull or lift the baby by the grip.

schedule.what: With the parent's permission, put a finger in the baby's palm and feel the grip.

activities.record: Draw the baby's hand around your finger. Write how long the baby held on.

setup.art: A girl washing her hands with soap at a steel sink.
setup.caption: 1. Wash your hands with soap.

setup.art: A small finger laid across a newborn baby's open palm, and the baby's tiny fingers closing around the finger, with a grown-up holding the baby.
setup.caption: 2. Lay one finger across the baby's palm. Feel the fingers close.

flow.do: Your child washes their hands with soap. Ask the baby's parent for permission.
flow.say: We must wash our hands first, because tiny babies catch germs easily.
flow.kid: Wash your hands with soap first.

flow.do: With the parent holding the baby, your child lays one finger gently across the baby's open palm, and waits.
flow.say: Put one finger gently across the baby's palm. Don't push. Just wait. What does the baby do?
flow.kid: Put one finger in the baby's palm. Wait. What happens?

ask.q: Did the baby decide to hold on?
good: No, the hand closed by itself.

flow.parent: In a baby under about three months, the fingers usually close around the finger at once. This grip fades by about four to six months, and then the baby learns to reach and hold on purpose.

flow.do: Talk about it afterwards.
flow.say: Nobody taught the baby to grip. Who else is born knowing how to do something?
flow.kid: Who taught the baby to grip? What else are babies born knowing?

check.q: Why does a newborn baby grip a finger?
options: Someone taught her
She is born able to do it
She has watched others do it
check.why: Every healthy baby is born with this grip. It is there from the first day, before the baby has learned anything.

activities.title: Born Ready for Any Language: can you say 'zh'?
activities.context: In this activity you try to say a sound from Tamil and Malayalam, the 'zh' in 'Tamizh' and 'mazhai'. You find out who you know can say it easily, and who learned it as a baby.

materials.item: a family member who speaks Tamil or Malayalam, or a phone recording of these words

schedule.what: Listen to the 'zh' sound, try it five times, and ask three family members to try it too.

activities.record: A table: each person's name, the language they heard as a baby, and whether the 'zh' sound was easy, a bit hard or very hard. A grown-up can write the names.

setup.art: A drawing of a mouth from the side, with the tip of the tongue curled up and back towards the roof of the mouth.
setup.caption: 1. To say 'zh', curl the tip of your tongue up and back, and let the sound flow.

setup.art: A table on paper with three rows, one for each person you ask, and ticks for 'easy', 'a bit hard' and 'very hard'.
setup.caption: 2. Ask each person to try it. Write down who found it easy.

flow.do: Listen to someone say 'Tamizh' (the name of the Tamil language) and 'mazhai' (rain) and 'vaazhaipazham' (banana).
flow.say: Listen to this sound. It is in Tamil and Malayalam. 'Tamizh'. 'Mazhai'. Can you hear the 'zh'?
flow.kid: Listen. 'Tamizh'. 'Mazhai'. Can you hear the 'zh' sound?
flow.parent: The sound is made by curling the tip of the tongue up and back, and letting the sound flow without touching. If nobody at home speaks Tamil or Malayalam, many free videos and dictionary apps say these words aloud.

flow.do: Your child tries the words five times.
flow.say: Your turn. Curl your tongue up and back. Try 'mazhai' five times. Is it easy or hard?
flow.kid: Curl your tongue up and back. Say 'mazhai' five times.

flow.do: Ask three people you know, family or friends, to try. For each one, write down the language they heard as a baby, and whether 'zh' was easy.
flow.say: Let's ask three people. What language did each of them hear as a baby? Was the sound easy for them?
flow.kid: Ask three people to try. Which language did they hear as a baby?
flow.parent: Write the table for your child. Anyone who speaks Tamil or Malayalam will find it easy. Others may find it hard, and that is fine.

flow.do: Look at the table together.
flow.say: Who found it easy? Did they hear Tamil or Malayalam as babies? Were they born knowing the sound, or did they learn it?
flow.kid: Who found it easy? Did they learn the sound as a baby?

check.q: A baby is born in Bengaluru to a family who speak Malayalam at home. Which sounds will she learn to say easily?
options: Only Kannada sounds, because she was born in Bengaluru
The sounds of Malayalam, the language she hears every day
No sounds, until she goes to school
check.why: Every baby is born ready to learn any language. She learns the sounds she hears every day, so she will say the Malayalam 'zh' easily.

flow.parent: Babies a few months old can hear the difference between sounds from many languages. By about one year, they hear best the sounds of the language around them. Scientists like Janet Werker found this.

games.title: Born Ready, Learn Steady: a race through the first year
games.context: This is a board race. Each player is a baby animal. Some cards show born-with know-how, which works at once. Other cards show learning, which takes time but helps when something new happens.

setup.art: A paper board of 20 squares in a snake shape, from 'Born' to 'One year old', with squares 5, 10 and 15 marked 'Say it!' and small counters made of coins or buttons at the start.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a board of 20 squares, from 'Born' to 'One year old'. Put your counters on 'Born'.

setup.art: A child turning over a card that says 'Street light: the hatchling crawls the wrong way. Go back 2', while another child moves a button counter.
setup.caption: 2. Take turns turning over a card, and move as it says.

printables.title: 16 race cards, with the move on the back

items.f: You are a spiderling. You spin your first web, with no teacher.
items.b: Born ready. Move forward 3.

items.f: You are a calf. You stand up an hour after you are born.
items.b: Born ready. Move forward 3.

items.f: You are a turtle hatchling. You crawl to the bright sea.
items.b: Born ready. Move forward 3.

img.credit: Teja Yantrapalli, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: You are a baby. You drink milk on your first day.
items.b: Born ready. Move forward 3.

items.f: You are a baby. You grip a grown-up's finger tight.
items.b: Born ready. Move forward 2.

items.f: You are a turtle hatchling. A street light is brighter than the sea, and you crawl to it.
items.b: Born-with know-how fooled by something new. Go back 2.

img.credit: Teja Yantrapalli, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: You are a spiderling. Wind tears your web in the night.
items.b: Spin a new one in the same place. Move forward 1.

items.f: You are a kitten. Your first pounce misses the leaf.
items.b: Learning takes tries. Stay where you are this turn.

items.f: You are a kitten. You watch your mother hunt, then try again.
items.b: You learned. Move forward 3.

items.f: You are a baby. You try to walk and fall down.
items.b: Learning takes tries. Stay where you are this turn.

items.f: You are a baby. You take your first steps after months of trying.
items.b: You learned. Move forward 3.

items.f: You are a crow chick. A new balcony starts putting out rice.
items.b: You learn the new place and time. Move forward 3.

items.f: You are a chick. You miss most grains on your first day.
items.b: Born ready, but your aim needs practice. Move forward 1.

items.f: You are a chick. After a few days of pecking, you hit most grains.
items.b: Practice made your aim better. Move forward 2.

items.f: You are a baby. You hear your family talk every day.
items.b: You are learning your language. Move forward 2.

items.f: You are a weaver bird. Your first nest is untidy.
items.b: Weave again. Practice makes it neater. Move forward 1.

img.credit: Parth Kansara, CC BY, via iNaturalist

printables.title: A board of 20 squares to draw on paper
items: Square 5: Say it! Tell one thing you learned to do. Then move forward 1.
Square 10: Say it! Tell one thing you learned to do. Then move forward 1.
Square 15: Say it! Tell one thing you learned to do. Then move forward 1.

rules: Print the board, or draw 20 squares on a big sheet of paper, in a snake shape. Write 'Born' on the first square and 'One year old' on the last. Number the squares.
Each player uses a coin or a button as a counter, and starts on 'Born'.
Mix the cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Turn over the top card, read the front aloud, then read the back and move as it says. You can never go back past 'Born'.
Put used cards at the bottom of the pile, so the pile never runs out.
If you land on a 'Say it!' square, tell the others one thing you learned to do, then move forward 1. This extra move does not count as landing again.
The first player to reach or pass 'One year old' wins. With two players, you can also play on until both reach the end.

flow.do: 1. Print or draw the board of 20 squares. 2. Cut out the 16 cards. 3. Give each player a coin or a button.
flow.say: Let's make the board. Twenty squares, from the day you are born to your first birthday.
flow.kid: Draw 20 squares. Start on 'Born'.

flow.do: Play. On each card, ask: is this born-with know-how, or learning?
flow.say: A street light fooled the hatchling! Was that born-with know-how or learning? Why did it go wrong?
flow.kid: Read your card. Is it born ready, or learning? Move.

ask.q: Why did the street light card send you back?
good: The hatchling follows the brightest light, and the street light was brighter.
Her born-with know-how did not expect a street light.

flow.do: Talk about it after the game.
flow.say: Born-with know-how works at once. Learning takes tries. Which one helped when something new happened, like the new balcony with rice?
flow.kid: Which helped with something new: born ready, or learning?

check.q: A crow chick finds a new balcony that puts out rice. How does she come back at the right time?
options: She was born knowing about that balcony
She learns where and when the rice comes
The rice calls her
check.why: Nobody is born knowing about one balcony. The crow learns the place and the time by going there and finding food. Learning helps with new things.

flow.parent: Born-with know-how is ready on the first day, but it was made for the world the animal's parents lived in. Learning is slower, but it helps an animal with things that are new.

games.title: Turtle Run: find the sea in the dark
games.context: This is a game about olive ridley turtle hatchlings on the beaches of Odisha and Chennai. Hatchlings are born knowing to crawl towards the brighter sky over the sea. In a dark room, a torch is the bright sky over the sea. Then a street light comes on. You play together as one clutch of hatchlings, and try to reach the sea on as many nights as you can.

setup.art: A dark room with a child crouched on a mat at one end, and at the other end a torch standing on the floor, leaning on a book and pointing at the ceiling to make a soft glow, with a grown-up beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Make the room dark. Stand one torch low at one end, pointing up. That is the sea.

setup.art: The same room, with a second torch shining brightly from a chair by the side wall, and a child crawling towards it instead of the low glow.
setup.caption: 2. On a 'street light' card, the grown-up switches on a second, brighter torch standing on a chair by the side wall. Which way do the hatchlings go?

printables.title: 8 night cards, with what to do on the back

items.f: A quiet night. Only the sea shines.
items.b: Only the sea torch is on. Crawl to the sea.

items.f: The Moon is up over the sea.
items.b: Only the sea torch is on, a little brighter. Crawl to the sea.

items.f: A shop behind the beach turns on its lights.
items.b: Turn on the side torch, bright. Crawl to the brightest light you see.

items.f: A street light comes on near the sand.
items.b: Turn on the side torch, bright. Crawl to the brightest light you see.

items.f: Volunteers ask the shops to switch off their lights.
items.b: Turn off the side torch. Crawl to the sea.

items.f: A family on the beach shines a phone torch.
items.b: Turn on the side torch for a short time, then off. Crawl towards the brightest light you see. When the side torch goes off, turn to the sea.

items.f: Clouds cover the Moon.
items.b: Only the sea torch is on, dim. Crawl slowly to the sea.

items.f: A shop puts a dark shade over the bright sign near the beach.
items.b: Turn on the side torch, but cover it with a cloth so it is dimmer than the sea. Crawl to the brightest light you see.

rules: Clear the floor, so nobody can bump into furniture. Make the room as dark as you safely can.
Never shine a torch into anyone's eyes. Point both torches at the ceiling or the wall.
Stand one torch on the floor at one end of the room, leaning on a book so it points up and makes a soft glow. That is the sea. Stand the second torch on a chair by the side wall.
One grown-up reads the cards and switches the torches on and off. The players are hatchlings. They crouch on a mat at the far end, with eyes closed.
The grown-up reads a night card aloud and does what the back says.
The hatchlings open their eyes and crawl slowly towards the brightest light they see. No running.
If the hatchlings reach the sea torch, you win that night. If they reach the side torch, the night is lost.
After all 8 cards, count the nights you won. Which cards made you lose a night? Then shuffle and play again, and try to win more nights.

flow.do: 1. Clear the floor and make the room dark. 2. Stand the sea torch on the floor at one end, and the second torch on a chair by the side wall. 3. The hatchlings crouch at the far end.
flow.say: You are baby turtles, just out of the sand. Nobody can show you the way to the sea. You only know one thing: crawl to the brightest light.
flow.kid: You are a baby turtle. Crawl to the brightest light you see.
flow.parent: Keep the floor clear and keep the crawling slow, so nobody is hurt in the dark. With only two of you, the grown-up is the sea and the reader, and the child is the hatchling.

flow.do: Read each night card and do what the back says. Count the nights you reach the sea.
flow.say: A street light comes on! Which way will you crawl?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Crawl slowly to the brightest light.

ask.q: Why did the hatchlings crawl to the street light?
good: They follow the brightest light, and the street light was brighter than the sea.

flow.parent: On a dark beach, the sky over the sea is usually brighter than the land behind the beach. Hatchlings are born knowing to crawl towards it. Lights from roads, houses and shops can lead them the wrong way.

flow.do: Talk about it.
flow.say: The hatchlings were born knowing the way. What can people do so that their born-with know-how works?
flow.kid: How can people help baby turtles find the sea?

check.q: A shop near a turtle beach puts a dark shade over the bright sign. What will the hatchlings do?
options: Crawl to the shop, because it is still a light
Crawl to the sea, because the sea sky is now the brightest light
Stay in the sand for ever
check.why: Hatchlings crawl towards the brightest light. When the light on land is dimmed, the brighter sky over the sea leads them the right way.

projects.title: Night Light Count: three nights at the window
projects.context: Turtle hatchlings are born knowing to crawl to the brightest light, which is usually the sky over the sea. In this project you count the lights you can see from your window at night, for three nights, and make a poster about which lights could be switched off.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and colours, for the poster

schedule.what: At 8 in the evening, count the lights you can see from one window for 5 minutes. Sort them: street lights, homes, shops and signs, vehicles.
Count again from the same window at the same time. Which lights are on every night?
Count for the last time. Then make a poster: which lights could be dimmed or switched off near a turtle beach?

projects.record: A tally table for each night, and a poster.

setup.art: A child at a flat window at night, looking out at street lights, lit windows and a glowing shop sign, with a notebook of tally marks.
setup.caption: 1. Look out of one window at 8 in the evening. Count the lights for 5 minutes.

setup.art: A child's poster showing a dark beach with turtle hatchlings crawling to a glowing sea, and a shop behind with its lights crossed out.
setup.caption: 2. On day 3, make a poster about lights and turtles.

flow.do: At 8 in the evening, your child counts the lights they see from one window, for 5 minutes. They make tally marks in four groups: street lights, homes, shops and signs, vehicles.
flow.say: Let's count the lights we can see. Make a tally mark for each one. Is it a street light, a home, a shop or a vehicle?
flow.kid: Count the lights you see. Make a tally mark for each one.
flow.parent: Stay with your child at the window or balcony. A child should never lean out. If your window shows only a few lights, count what you can. Fewer lights is fine.

flow.do: On day 2, count again from the same window at the same time.
flow.say: Same window, same time. Which lights are on again tonight?
flow.kid: Count again. Which lights are on every night?
flow.wait: Do this on day 2, at the same time as day 1.

flow.do: On day 3, count for the last time. Then your child makes a poster: which lights near a beach could be switched off or shaded in turtle season?
flow.say: If our street were next to a turtle beach, which of these lights would lead the hatchlings the wrong way? Which ones could we switch off?
flow.kid: Count once more. Then make a poster to help baby turtles.

check.q: Why do lights near a beach matter to turtle hatchlings?
options: Hatchlings like to read at night
Hatchlings are born knowing to crawl to the brightest light, so a bright light on land leads them the wrong way
Lights make the sand warm
check.why: Hatchlings crawl towards the brightest light, which is usually the sky over the sea. A bright light on land can lead them away from the sea.

challenges.title: Beak Weaving: weave like a baya
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A male baya weaver weaves a hanging nest of grass strips using only his beak and feet. Now you weave a small mat from paper strips, using only the thumb and first finger of one hand, like a beak.
challenges.problem: Can you weave a small mat from paper strips, with one hand as a beak, that stays together when you lift it by the pencil and holds 10 chana lying on it?
constraints: Weave with only the thumb and first finger of one hand. Your other hand may only hold the pencil, like a branch.
Use 24 paper strips, each about as wide as your finger and as long as a ruler. Twelve are for the first mat and twelve for the second.
Fold 6 strips over the pencil so they hang down. Weave the other 6 across them, over and under.
materials: newspaper or old magazine pages cut into 24 strips
a pencil or a steel tumbler to weave around
general: Lay a strip across the hanging strips, over one and under the next, like a mat.
Push each new strip up close to the one before, so there are no big gaps.
Tuck the ends in tightly, so the weave does not come apart.
creative: Twist each strip into a thin rope first, so it is stronger and easier to tuck.
Tie a knot by looping a strip around itself, the way a weaver bird knots his first strips onto a branch.
challenges.your_turn: Weave your mat. Lay it flat and put 10 chana on it. Do any fall through? Then weave a second mat. Is it better than your first? What did you learn from the first try?

setup.art: A child's hand pinching a paper strip between thumb and first finger like a beak, weaving it over and under strips hanging from a pencil held in the other hand.
setup.caption: 1. Hang strips from a pencil. Weave with your thumb and first finger only.

setup.art: A small woven paper mat lying flat on a table with 10 chana grains on it and none on the table below.
setup.caption: 2. Lift the mat by the pencil, then lay it flat and put 10 chana on it. Do any fall through?

flow.do: Read the challenge together. Talk about how a baya weaves his nest with only his beak and feet.
flow.say: A baya weaves a hanging nest with only his beak. Can you weave a mat with only two fingers of one hand?
flow.kid: Weave a mat with only two fingers. Can it hold 10 chana?

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the strips and folds the first 6 over the pencil. Your child weaves the first mat. Help only with the cutting and folding.
flow.say: Where will you start? How will you keep the strips from coming apart?
flow.kid: Weave your first mat. Use only two fingers.
flow.parent: Let your child try their own way first, even if it falls apart. A first try that fails teaches the most for the second try.

flow.do: 1. Lift the first mat by the pencil. Does it stay together? 2. Lay it flat and put 10 chana on it. 3. Weave a second mat. 4. Test it too.
flow.say: How many chana stayed on? Now weave a second one. What will you do differently?
flow.kid: Test it. Then weave a second mat. Is it better?

ask.q: Why was your second mat better?
good: I learned to tuck the ends in tight.
I knew where to start this time.
My fingers got better at it.

check.q: A young weaver bird's first nests are often untidy. Why are his later nests better?
options: He gets a new beak
He gets better with practice
Other birds build them for him
check.why: A weaver bird is born ready to weave, but practice makes his nests neater. Your second mat was probably better for the same reason.

items.p: A baby spider spins her first web. Who taught her how?
opts: Nobody. She was born knowing how
The other spiders in the house
items.why: In many kinds of spider, the mother is gone before the babies hatch. Each spiderling spins her first web with no teacher. This is instinct.

items.p: Sort these baby animals: can do this on the first day, or needs months to learn?
items: a hatchling crawling to the sea
items.why: A spiderling, a calf and a hatchling do these on the first day. Talking, walking and hunting take months of learning and practice.
items.art: Six small drawings: a spiderling, a talking baby, a calf, a kitten and a lizard, a turtle hatchling, and a baby walking.

items.p: Remember the stop test. Draw your leg three times: relaxed, trying to stop, and pulling your fingers. Show how big each kick was with an arrow.
items.a: Three legs. Usually a long arrow for relaxed, a shorter arrow or none for trying to stop, and the longest arrow for pulling.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a different arrow for each way, and matches the results table.
items.art: Three empty boxes in a row, labelled 'Relaxed', 'Trying to stop' and 'Pulling fingers'.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: in the stop test, could you stop your knee kick by trying? What did you see?
items.a: Not always. When I tried hard not to kick, my leg still kicked on some taps, but smaller.
items.why: A strong answer uses the result from the test, with numbers if possible, and says that the kick happens before you decide.

items.p: Humans have no instincts. People have to learn everything.
items.why: False. Human babies are born able to suck, grip and cry, and everyone has reflexes like sneezing and the knee kick.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to what they can do from birth.
items.why: All four can do these from the very first day, with nobody to teach them. These are instincts.
items.art: Four baby animals on the left and four actions on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Label the two columns of this picture: 'born with it' and 'learned it'.
a: born with it: the baby gripping a finger and the spider spinning
learned it: the girl reading and the boy riding a cycle
items.why: The baby's grip and the spider's web need no teaching. Reading and cycling must be learned.
items.art: A picture split in two, with a baby gripping a finger and a spider spinning on one side, a girl reading and a boy on a cycle on the other, and an empty label above each side.

items.p: Something an animal can do from birth, without being taught, is called an ________.
items.why: An instinct is something an animal can do from birth, the first time, with no teaching.

items.p: Lakshmi, aged 7, lives in Chennai. A spider has spun a round web on the balcony grill.

views.says: Let's sweep the web away. It is messy.
Leave it. The spider spun the web with nobody to teach her, and the web catches mosquitoes.
Leave it tonight so we can watch how she mends it. We can look again tomorrow.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one good thing about another person's idea.
items.a: Any side, with a reason. For example: 'I agree with the grandmother, because the web catches mosquitoes. But the mother's idea means we can still watch the spider.'
items.why: A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and is fair to another point of view.

items.p: A girl does the stop test. Her knee kicked 5 times relaxed, 3 times when she tried to stop it, and 5 times when she pulled her fingers. How many kicks in all?
items.why: 5 and 3 make 8, and 5 more makes 13. Even when she tried to stop it, her leg kicked 3 times.

items.p: Three of these are born-with actions. Which one is learned?
opts: A blink when something flies at your eye
items.why: Sneezing, blinking at something flying at your eye and the knee kick are reflexes. Writing your name has to be learned.

items.p: Sabari, a boy of five, says, 'I was born knowing how to whistle.' His grandmother remembers him practising for two weeks. Who is right, and how do you know?
items.a: His grandmother is right. If Sabari had to practise for two weeks before any whistle came out, he learned it.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence: a born-with action works on the first try, but Sabari needed many tries.

items.p: A chick pecks at grains on her first day, but misses many. After a few days she misses fewer. What does this show?
opts: Pecking is born ready, and practice makes her aim better
items.why: Nobody teaches a chick to peck, so pecking is an instinct. Her aim gets better with practice, so it is a bit of both.

items.p: Draw a round spider web, the kind many spiders spin at dusk. Show the spokes and the spiral.
items.a: A web with lines going out from the middle like the spokes of a wheel, and a spiral going round and round across the spokes.
items.why: Every round web has spokes from the middle and a spiral thread. A spiderling spins this pattern with nobody to copy.
items.art: An empty box for drawing, with two corners of a balcony grill drawn at the edges.

items.p: Put a baby's skills in order, from the earliest to the latest.
items.why: A baby grips from birth. Most babies sit up at around six months, walk at around one year and run after that.

items.p: An old person's knee kicks when it is tapped, just like a child's.
items.why: True. The knee kick is a reflex people are born with, and it stays at every age.

items.p: Label the path of the knee kick message: knee, backbone, leg muscle.
a: backbone: where the message goes and comes straight back
leg muscle: which tightens and makes the leg kick
items.why: The tap stretches the leg muscle. A message runs to the spinal cord in the backbone and straight back, so the muscle tightens before you decide anything.
items.art: A side view of a child sitting with a leg hanging, with an arrow from the knee up to the backbone and another arrow back down to the front of the leg, and three empty label lines.

items.p: Match each skill to how it is learned.
pairs: A crow coming to the rice window
items.why: All four are learned. Some learning is by watching, some by hearing, some by trying again and again.
items.art: Four pictures on the left and four short phrases on the right, mixed up.

items.p: A very quick action the body does by itself, like a sneeze, is called a ________.
items.why: A reflex happens by itself, before you decide. Sneezing, blinking and the knee kick are reflexes.

items.p: A blink when something flies at your face happens before you decide to blink.
items.why: True. A blink is a reflex. It happens by itself, before you decide.

items.p: Three children argue about a baya weaver who weaves a hanging grass nest.

views.says: It is instinct. Nobody teaches him to weave.
It is learning. Young weavers make messy nests and get better.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use one fact from this unit. Then say what the others got right.
items.a: Many children agree with Farhan: the weaver is born ready to weave, and his nests get neater with practice. Meera is right that nobody teaches him, and Thenmozhi is right that practice helps.
items.why: A strong answer uses a fact, such as young weavers' nests getting neater, and gives each view its fair part.

items.p: In the stop test, pulling your hooked fingers usually made the kick bigger. Why do you think that happened?
items.a: For example: when I was busy pulling, I was not holding my leg stiff, so the kick could happen fully.
items.why: A strong answer links the bigger kick to the leg being loose, because the mind was busy with the hands.

items.p: Anjali's baby cousin was born in Kolkata to a Telugu-speaking family. The family speaks only Telugu at home. Which language will the baby speak first?
opts: Bengali, because she was born in Kolkata
Telugu, because that is what she hears every day
English, because babies are born knowing English
items.why: Babies are born ready to learn any language. They learn the one they hear around them every day.

items.p: Arabella, a spider in a space station, spun a messy first web. Her next webs were much better. Was web spinning an instinct or learned for her? Explain.
items.a: Both. She was born knowing how to spin, so she spun a web straight away. But she did better after trying, so she also changed what she did.
items.why: A strong answer sees both parts: the know-how she was born with, and the way she got better in a strange place.

items.p: Draw a cartoon in two boxes. Box 1: something you could do as a newborn baby. Box 2: something you learned this year.
items.a: Box 1 might show a baby gripping, crying or drinking milk. Box 2 might show reading, swimming or cycling.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one born-with action and one learned skill, and the child can say which is which.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, labelled 'As a newborn baby' and 'This year'.

items.p: Sort: instinct, learned, or both?
items: a calf standing on his first day
items.why: A calf standing and a spiderling spinning need no teaching. A dog sitting and a child cycling are learned. A kitten and a chick start with an instinct and get better with practice.
items.art: Six small pictures of the animals and children in the list.

items.p: If something is an instinct, practice can never make it any better.
items.why: False. Many instincts get better with practice. A chick's aim improves, young weavers' nests get neater, and Arabella spun better webs after her first one.

items.p: This picture shows a baby walking at one year old. Label the part she was born with and the part she learned.
a: born with it: the stepping movements of her legs
learned it: balancing and walking without falling
items.why: Newborn babies make stepping movements when held up. Balancing and walking on their own take about a year of practice.
items.art: A baby taking wobbly steps towards a grown-up's open arms, with two arrows pointing at her legs and at her held-out arms for balance, and two empty labels.

items.p: Which one is not learned?
opts: A crow coming to the window that gives rice
A newborn baby turning to a touch on her cheek

open_questions.q: How do genes carry the know-how to spin a web of the right shape?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that each kind of spider spins her own kind of web, and that this is passed on from parents. Nobody knows how tiny instructions inside cells become the steps of spinning a web.

open_questions.q: What does a spider sense and think while she spins?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can watch every step a spider takes. What it is like to be a spider spinning a web, and how much she plans, are still argued about.

open_questions.q: How much of what a person is like comes from birth, and how much is learned?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists agree that both matter, and that they work together. Exactly how much each matters for any one thing, such as being good at music, is still argued about.

maths.problem: Four people in a family did the stop test while trying not to kick. Their kicks out of 5 were 3, 4, 2 and 5. Who kicked most? How many kicks in all?
maths.answer: The person with 5 kicked most. There were 14 kicks in all.
maths.explain: 5 is the biggest number. 3 and 4 make 7, and 2 more makes 9, and 5 more makes 14. Out of 20 taps, the legs kicked 14 times, even with everyone trying to stop.
maths.context: This is about the stop test, done by a whole family.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the whole family's kicks shows that the kick usually happens, whoever is trying to stop it.

maths.problem: A spider has 8 legs. Three spiderlings come out of an egg bag. How many legs do they have in all?
maths.explain: There are 3 groups of 8 legs. 8 and 8 make 16, and 8 more makes 24.
maths.context: This is about baby spiders, who are born with 8 legs and the know-how to spin.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups is quicker than counting every leg.

maths.problem: A girl counts lights from her window. Night 1: 12 lights. Night 2: 12 lights. Night 3: 9 lights. How many fewer lights on night 3 than night 1?
maths.explain: Count up from 9 to 12: 10, 11, 12. That is 3. Maybe three shops closed early.
maths.context: This is about the Night Light Count, where you count lights from your window for three nights.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the nights shows which lights change and which are on every night.

maths.problem: In the Turtle Run game, 4 hatchlings crawl to the sea when the street light is off. When it is on, only 1 reaches the sea. How many fewer reach the sea with the light on?
maths.explain: 4 take away 1 is 3. The light led 3 hatchlings the wrong way.
maths.context: This is about the Turtle Run game, where hatchlings crawl to the brightest light.
maths.why_maths: Taking away shows how many hatchlings the light on land led the wrong way.

Patellar (knee-jerk) reflex: a monosynaptic stretch reflex through the spinal cord, present in newborns.
Jendrassik manoeuvre: pulling hooked fingers apart makes the knee-jerk reflex larger; tensing the leg can reduce it.
Newborn reflexes: palmar grasp (fades by about 4 to 6 months), rooting, sucking, stepping.

J. F. Werker and R. C. Tees, 'Cross-language speech perception', Infant Behavior and Development 7 (1984): infants of 6 to 8 months tell apart Hindi and Salish sound pairs that adults of another language cannot; by 10 to 12 months this fades.

Hatchling sea turtles orient towards the brighter, lower horizon over the sea; artificial lights misdirect them (sea-finding studies, for example by Michael Salmon and colleagues).

roots.context: We have met animals who are born knowing and animals who learn, and tried to stop our own knee kick. Now we ask what this tells us about who is in charge of a body.

deep_truth.truth: When you tried hard not to kick, your leg often kicked anyway. Nobody ever taught you that kick, and trying could not switch it off. It was ready in your body on the day you were born. So knowing how to do something can come before any lesson.
deep_truth.habit: We think that knowing how to do something always starts with being taught. But some know-how is ready in the body at birth, like the knee kick and a spider's web, and this know-how works without any lesson.
deep_truth.evidence: In the stop test, the knee often kicked even when the child tried hard not to kick, and kicked biggest when the mind was busy pulling the fingers. Spiderlings spin the web of their own kind with no teacher.

three.who_am_i: You are the one who decides, and you are also a body that knew how to grip, sneeze and kick before you ever decided anything.
three.what_is_life: Every living being starts life already knowing some things, and then keeps learning. A spider, a calf and a baby all do both.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of know-how passed from parents to young, in every web on every balcony and every nest in every palm tree.

roots.thread: Every spider alive today got her web know-how in her genes from her parents, who got theirs from their parents. Nobody wrote it down, and no spider taught another. It travelled inside bodies, from one life to the next, for millions of years. So one small spider on a balcony grill carries the know-how of a long line of spiders before her. Your knee kick and your grip came to you the same way, down a long line of people and the animals before them.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son to split a tiny banyan seed. The son sees nothing inside. Uddalaka says the whole great banyan tree grows from that nothing you cannot see.
teachings.link: A spiderling's know-how to spin cannot be seen inside her either. Yet the whole round web comes out of her, the first time she spins.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar says: learn well, without mistakes, what is worth learning. Then live by what you have learned.
teachings.link: Some things we are born with, like the knee kick. But most skills, like a kolam or a language, have to be learned well, through practice.

teachings.teaching: In this old Greek book, Socrates asks a boy who has never studied geometry a series of questions. The boy works out a hard answer. Socrates says that some knowing was already in him before any lesson.
teachings.link: Scientists today say that born-with know-how is passed on in genes from parents, not remembered from before. But Plato also noticed that we do not start with nothing.

science.text: Spiderlings spin the web of their own kind with no teacher, and newborn babies have reflexes such as gripping and sucking.
How genes carry know-how such as a web pattern, from parent to young, is not yet understood.

other_view.who: John Locke, an English thinker, in 1690
other_view.view: Locke said a baby's mind at birth is like a blank sheet of white paper, and everything we know comes from what we see, hear and do. Many people still think most of what makes a person comes from learning, and in a way they are right: most of our skills are learned.

practice.title: Born-With Breath
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Notice your breath going in and out. Nobody taught you to breathe. You did it from your first minute. Now slow it down on purpose. how_we_found_out.story: In 1973, astronauts lived for weeks on Skylab, a space station going round the Earth. Judith Miles, a high school student from Lexington in the United States, asked a question. Could a spider spin her web in space, where nothing has weight? On Earth, a spider uses her own weight as she drops and swings on her threads. Many people expected the web-spinning would go wrong without it. NASA sent up two garden spiders, Arabella and Anita, and the astronaut Owen Garriott watched them. At first, Arabella spun a messy, uneven web. But her next webs looked much more like the round webs that spiders spin on Earth. Anita spun a fine web too. The spiders were born knowing how to spin. Arabella's later webs show that her spinning could change a little in a strange new place.
how_we_found_out.who: Judith Miles, a high school student who suggested the test, with NASA and the astronaut Owen Garriott, who watched the spiders Arabella and Anita
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a spider's web-spinning is a fixed set of steps that would fail in a strange place with no weight. Arabella's first web was messy, but her next webs were much better.
how_we_found_out.art: Two garden spiders in small clear boxes floating inside a space station, one with a round web, and an astronaut looking in through the window, with a photo of a smiling girl student pinned beside the boxes.

playtest: Walked through the unit as a parent and child in a flat. The 20-square board is now written out square by square, with three Say-it squares, and the race rules say what happens at the start and the end. The Turtle Run game could never have a winner, because everyone crawls to the same light; it is now one shared goal, with torches a single grown-up can switch, and a shaded-sign card.
